overview: The Ais lived along Florida’s central Atlantic coast south of Cape Canaveral. Fishing and water travel supported their communities, while encounters with shipwrecks and foreign vessels helped their leaders build influence during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

periods.title: Coastal livelihoods and Atlantic encounters
periods.summary: The Ais adapted established maritime skills to salvage, exchange and negotiations with Europeans. Ferdinando’s research emphasizes their continuing regional influence into the beginning of the eighteenth century, despite late-seventeenth-century raids.

periods.title: Raiding, refuge and dispersal
periods.summary: Slave raids drove major movements through southern Florida. Ais people appear among refugees near St. Augustine in 1711 and in later mission lists. These records describe survivors and changing communities, rather than a single securely dated conquest of an Ais state.

items.text: At Herman’s Bay on Hutchinson Island, site 8SL1146, excavators found evidence of a house, a cooking hearth and discarded animal remains. The project places these traces in the Okeechobee period, about 1000 to 1513 CE. They illuminate the region’s earlier coastal life, but the report does not identify the occupants specifically as Ais.

Herman’s Bay animal bones point to fishing and turtle consumption, with resources drawn especially from the Indian River estuary and Atlantic shore. Very small schooling fish led researchers to infer fine-mesh nets or similar gear. The bones are observed evidence; the proposed equipment is an interpretation, not a surviving net.

A community excavation led by Alan Brech at Cape Canaveral’s site 8BR1936 recovered pottery, bone and shell beads, shell tools and food remains. Field Manor reports work from 2015 to 2019 and a proposed identification with Savochequeya, a village on Mexía’s 1605 map. That town identification remains a proposal.

At the same site, dark post molds marked the positions of decayed wooden supports; pits and hearths also survived. These soil traces help reconstruct buildings and household activity even where the wood has disappeared. They offer a different kind of evidence from the names and routes recorded by European visitors.

Three early glass beads and European metal were reported alongside local pottery and shell objects at 8BR1936. A possible copper-alloy button was also identified. The finds show access to imported materials, but the button’s identification is tentative and individual objects cannot establish the route by which every item reached the settlement.

At Jece in 1696, Dickinson recorded baskets of dried berries arriving from other towns and being delivered to a chief. He thought these deliveries were tribute. His observation documents stored food and movement between settlements; the explanation as tribute is his interpretation, not an independently recorded rule for every Ais community.

Ferdinando argues that the Ais used existing aquatic skills to recover goods and castaways from wrecked Spanish, French, English and Dutch ships. Redistributing these resources to other Native communities, St. Augustine and passing Europeans increased their influence. Salvage was part of an active political economy, rather than simply the collection of accidental treasure.

Dickinson saw tools, knives, wooden ship fittings and a razor bearing the name Thomas Foster at Jece. These objects give his account a concrete material dimension. He did not learn the full history of their arrival, so the record cannot show whether each item came through wreck salvage, exchange or another encounter.

A resident of Jece told Dickinson that ambergris could buy a mirror, an axe, knives and tobacco at St. Augustine. The passage links a coastal resource with desired tools and consumer goods. It records one person’s expected exchange, not a fixed price list or proof that all residents traded on identical terms.

Maritime expertise also exposed Native people to enslavement. Ferdinando describes late-seventeenth-century English buccaneers capturing coastal divers for work on a wreck in the Bahamas and subsequently selling survivors in Caribbean markets. Skill could support local autonomy while also attracting coercive exploitation.

Worth identifies a 1711 town near St. Augustine containing more than a hundred Ais and other coastal refugees. The number describes a mixed community, not a census of all Ais people. Subsequent mission lists still named Ais, showing why a story of abrupt disappearance would conceal a documented history of survival and displacement.

ending.text: Raiding and displacement undermined the Ais coastal political order in the early eighteenth century. Ais survivors are documented near St. Augustine, but the evidence cited here does not establish one final dissolution year or trace every later family. Wider migrations to Cuba should not be converted into an unsupported claim that all Ais died or left together.
